title: Entanglement Geometry Beyond Polygons: Graph-Theoretic Entanglement Inequalities
problem: In a pure state of many parties, the entanglement of one party with the rest can never exceed the sum of the others' values. This polygon inequality is the oldest constraint of its kind. Cuts that separate larger groups obey constraints too, but which ones, and with what coefficients? Given a distinguished group of parties and any weighted list of other cuts, how much must the listed cuts be entangled, at least, if the distinguished one is?
result: For a distinguished pair of parties \(i,j\) the question is answered completely. Let \(W(u,v)\) be the total weight of the listed cuts that separate party \(u\) from party \(v\). The best constant \(\mu\) in \(\mu\,\mathcal E_{ij}\le\sum_Iw_I\mathcal E_I\) is the smallest \(W(x,\ell)\) with \(x\in\{i,j\}\) and \(\ell\) outside the pair. A refinement with three mutual-information terms gives the exact minimum of the weighted sum once the entropies of \(i\), \(j\) and \(ij\) are fixed. At most three independent shared pairs attain it. Around this result the paper derives inequalities for chains, cycles, hypergraphs and stars of cuts, a sharp bound for a single \(k\)-party cut against all of them, and exact or approximate descriptions of the states that reach equality.
significance: The answer is a minimum over pairs of parties, computable by inspection, and it is optimal for every weighted family. It also says which states are extremal: not exotic multipartite states but a few independent Bell-type bonds. That is a concrete instance of a familiar picture from holography, where entropies of cuts are modelled by the weight of bonds crossing them; here the bond picture is exact for the extremal value. The consequences include necessary bond dimensions for matrix product states and error estimates for sequential recovery.
limitations: The complete answer covers distinguished cuts of one or two parties; the paper leaves larger distinguished groups open. All statements use the von Neumann entropy of pure states. The proofs need strong subadditivity, which fails for other entropies such as the linear entropy. Several ingredients were known: the chain inequality is the Markov entropy decomposition, the average hierarchy follows from the symmetrized entropy cone, and the sharp \(k\)-party coefficient follows from a general result of Filmus on symmetric submodular functions, as the paper says. It is a single-author paper. The author states that Claude Opus 5.5 assisted with drafting, checking arguments, bibliographic research and three figures, and that it pointed out three of the references.

methods_basis: Based on the linked paper version. Derivations marked as editorial, and suggested uses in other problems, are editorial guidance rather than results of the paper.
description: For a pure state of \(n\) parties and a group \(I\) of them, write \(\mathcal E_I\) for the entropy of the group, which equals the entropy of its complement. Subadditivity gives the polygon inequality \(\mathcal E_{A_k}\le\sum_{j\ne k}\mathcal E_{A_j}\). The paper treats a group of parties as an edge or hyperedge of a graph and asks which lists of edges force a lower bound on their total entropy.

The first step beyond single parties is a chain. Adding up strong subadditivity along a line of parties makes the long blocks cancel, and leaves an exact identity: the entropies of neighbouring pairs minus the entropies of the interior parties equal a sum of conditional mutual informations. Equality therefore means that every step of the chain is an exact quantum Markov step. Closing the chain into a cycle gives \(2\,\mathcal E_{A_kA_{k+1}}\le\sum_j\mathcal E_{A_jA_{j+1}}\), an edge version of the polygon inequality. A hypergraph in which every party lies in an even number of hyperedges, or every party in an odd number, obeys the same polygon inequality.

Parity turns out to be sufficient but not necessary, and the two-party theorem explains why. What matters for a distinguished pair is only how often the listed cuts separate one of its members from some outside party. If some outside party \(\ell\) is separated from \(i\) by little weight, a Bell pair shared between \(i\) and \(\ell\) makes \(\mathcal E_{ij}\) positive at little cost, so the constant cannot be larger than that weight. The theorem says this obvious obstruction is the only one. A five-party star of pairs through a hub, with one of its pairs distinguished, has constant 2 although its degrees have mixed parity.

The refinement fixes the three entropies \(\mathcal E_i\), \(\mathcal E_j\) and \(\mathcal E_{ij}\), and with them the mutual informations between \(i\), \(j\) and the rest. It states \[W(i,j)\,\mathcal I(i{:}j)+r_i\,\mathcal I(i{:}R)+r_j\,\mathcal I(j{:}R)\le2\sum_Iw_I\mathcal E_I,\] where \(R\) is everything outside the pair and \(r_x=\min_\ell W(x,\ell)\). For the windows of length \(r\) around a ring this gives a cycle inequality for any two parties, adjacent or not, with a correction proportional to their mutual information that grows with their distance.

For larger distinguished groups the paper gives the sharp inequality \(2\binom{n-2}{k-1}\mathcal E_{I_k}\le\sum_{J_k}\mathcal E_{J_k}\) over all \(k\)-party cuts, and optimal constants for partial stars of cuts through one party. On the equality side, pure states that saturate the chain inequality are, up to local isometries, independent pure bonds between neighbours. Open cluster states saturate the hyperchain inequality while the chain inequality stays strict. Near equality in the cycle inequality implies closeness in trace distance to an exact equality state, with a bound that depends on neither the number of parties nor their dimensions.

methods.technique: Replacing a state by bond weights that never exceed its cut entropies
methods.explanation: The two-party theorem is proved by building, from the entropies of an arbitrary pure state, a set of nonnegative weights on pairs of parties. For every group of parties, the total weight of pairs it cuts is at most the group's entropy, and for the groups \(i\), \(j\) and \(ij\) it is exactly the entropy. Summing over the listed cuts then counts each pair by the weight that separates it, and the constant can be read off.
math: Order the outside parties and let \(P_\ell\) and \(Q_\ell\) be those before and after \(\ell\). Write \(D(\ell|U)=\mathcal E_{U\cup\ell}-\mathcal E_U\) for the entropy added by \(\ell\). For \(B\subseteq\{i,j\}\) average the two orders, \[L_\ell(B)=\tfrac12\bigl[D(\ell|P_\ell\cup B)+D(\ell|Q_\ell\cup B)\bigr].\] Strong subadditivity says that added entropy shrinks when the conditioning set grows. Summing over \(\ell\) in any subset \(U\) of the outside parties and telescoping gives \[\sum_{\ell\in U}L_\ell(B)\le\mathcal E_{U\cup B}-\mathcal E_B,\] with equality when \(U\) is everything outside the pair.

Purity supplies the missing relation: \(D(\ell|P_\ell\cup\{i\})=-D(\ell|Q_\ell\cup\{j\})\), because the complement of \(P_\ell\cup\{\ell,i\}\) is \(Q_\ell\cup\{j\}\). Hence \(L_\ell(\{j\})=-L_\ell(\{i\})\). Assign \[\lambda_{ij}=\tfrac12\mathcal I(i{:}j),\qquad\lambda_{x\ell}=\tfrac12\bigl[L_\ell(\emptyset)-L_\ell(\{x\})\bigr],\quad x\in\{i,j\},\] which are nonnegative. For a group \(I\) of outside parties the weight it cuts is \(\sum_{\ell\in I}(\lambda_{i\ell}+\lambda_{j\ell})=\sum_{\ell\in I}L_\ell(\emptyset)\le\mathcal E_I\).

For \(I=\{i\}\cup U\) the pairs \(i\ell\) with \(\ell\in U\) stop being cut and the pairs \(j\ell\) start. The change is \(\sum_{\ell\in U}(\lambda_{j\ell}-\lambda_{i\ell})=\sum_{\ell\in U}L_\ell(\{i\})\). Since \(\lambda_{ij}+\sum_\ell\lambda_{i\ell}=\mathcal E_i\), the cut weight is \(\mathcal E_i+\sum_{\ell\in U}L_\ell(\{i\})\le\mathcal E_I\). Complements cover all other groups. Therefore \[\sum_Iw_I\,\mathcal E_I\ge\sum_{u<v}\lambda_{uv}\,W(u,v),\] and \(W(x,\ell)\ge r_x\) with \(\sum_\ell\lambda_{x\ell}=\tfrac12\mathcal I(x{:}R)\) gives the refined inequality. Equality is reached by three independent bonds on \((i,j)\), \((i,\ell_i)\) and \((j,\ell_j)\), where \(\ell_x\) attains the minimum \(r_x\).
methods.transfer: The construction uses only strong subadditivity and the symmetry between a group and its complement, so it applies verbatim to any symmetric submodular function, for example cut functions of graphs. When a linear program over entropies is hard, dominating the entropies from below by a graph-cut function turns it into a minimum over pairs. The averaging over two opposite orders is what makes the weights consistent for both members of the pair. How to extend it to distinguished groups of three or more parties is the open problem.

methods.technique: Averaged strong subadditivity on the two sides of a cut
methods.explanation: The sharp bound for one \(k\)-party cut against all \(k\)-party cuts averages strong subadditivity over subsets of the cut and, separately, over subsets of its complement. Averages of a submodular function over subsets of fixed size form a concave sequence, so each average lies above the chord between its endpoints.
math: Fix a \(k\)-party group \(I\) and a group \(K\) of size \(s\) outside it. The averages of \(\mathcal E_{J\cup K}\) over the \(r\)-party subsets \(J\) of \(I\) are concave in \(r\), with endpoints \(\mathcal E_K\) and \(\mathcal E_{I\cup K}\). The chord bound, multiplied by \(\binom kr\), reads \[\binom{k-1}{r-1}\mathcal E_{I\cup K}+\binom{k-1}{r}\mathcal E_K\le\sum_{J\subseteq I,\,|J|=r}\mathcal E_{J\cup K}.\] The same argument over subsets \(K\) of the complement, where the endpoint entropies are \(0\) and \(\mathcal E_I\), bounds the sums of \(\mathcal E_K\) and of \(\mathcal E_{I\cup K}\) below by binomial multiples of \(\mathcal E_I\).

Choose \(r+s=k\) and sum. Every \(k\)-party group is counted once through its intersections with \(I\) and with the complement, and Vandermonde's identity gives \[2\binom{n-2}{k-1}\mathcal E_I\le\sum_{|J|=k}\mathcal E_J.\] A single entangled pair with one member in \(I\) and one outside gives equality: exactly \(2\binom{n-2}{k-1}\) groups contain one member of the pair, and each has entropy \(\mathcal E_I\).

The chain identity uses the same raw material without averaging. With conditional mutual information \(\mathcal I(X{:}Z|Y)\), \[\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\mathcal E_{A_jA_{j+1}}-\sum_{j=2}^{n-1}\mathcal E_{A_j}=\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}\mathcal I(A_1\cdots A_j{:}A_{j+2}|A_{j+1}),\] because the entropies of the growing prefixes cancel in pairs and the entropy of the whole pure state is zero. The right-hand side is a sum of nonnegative terms, which gives the inequality and its equality condition together.
methods.transfer: Concavity of subset averages is a quick way to obtain sharp symmetric inequalities for entropies, matroid ranks or cut functions, and the single-bond test is a quick way to see whether a proposed coefficient can be optimal. For a tensor network, inserting the entropies of contiguous blocks turns the same inequalities into necessary conditions on bond dimensions.
